QSBS EXCLUSION CALCULATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

How much of your QSBS gain is excluded?

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act replaced Section 1202's old all-or-nothing 5-year cliff with a tiered exclusion — 50% at 3 years, 75% at 4 years, 100% at 5 years — for stock acquired after July 4, 2025, and raised the per-issuer cap to $15 million. Stock from before that date still follows the old rule. This tool runs either rule on your own numbers.

Nothing is uploaded. Your numbers are read in this browser and never leave your device — see the privacy note in the footer.

1. Which rule applies

The rule depends on when you ACQUIRED the stock, not the year you sell it — stock acquired before the enactment date keeps the old all-or-nothing rule for its entire life.

2. Your numbers

The exclusion cap is the greater of a fixed dollar figure or 10 times your basis — a low basis (common for early founders/employees) usually means the fixed dollar cap governs.

Fill in the acquisition era, years held, gain, and basis, then click Calculate.

Result

What this does not cover

  • Not a full tax return. This computes one exclusion on one sale — not total tax liability, other deductions or credits, AMT, or state tax (state conformity to Section 1202 varies).
  • Does not verify QSBS eligibility. Original issuance, C-corp status, active-business requirements, and the gross-assets threshold at issuance are company-level facts this tool does not check.
  • No cumulative-cap tracking. The per-issuer cap is lifetime and cumulative across every sale of that issuer's stock; this tool assumes a single, first-ever sale against the cap.
  • No day-precision holding-period timing. The statute requires holding for MORE than the stated number of years; confirm your exact closing date against your acquisition date with a tax professional near a milestone.

Common questions

What changed about QSBS under OBBBA?

For stock acquired after July 4, 2025 (OBBBA's enactment date), Section 1202 gained a tiered holding-period schedule — 50% exclusion at 3 years, 75% at 4 years, 100% at 5 years — replacing the old all-or-nothing 5-year cliff. The per-issuer exclusion cap also rose from the greater of $10 million or 10x basis to the greater of $15 million or 10x basis.

Is there really no partial exclusion under the old rule?

Correct. For stock acquired on or before July 4, 2025, Section 1202 was strictly all-or-nothing: hold for more than 5 years and exclude 100% of eligible gain; sell even a day earlier and exclude 0%. There was no 3- or 4-year partial exclusion under the old rule at all.

How does the per-issuer cap work?

Eligible gain is capped at the greater of a fixed dollar figure ($10 million old rule, $15 million new rule) or 10 times your adjusted basis in the stock — whichever is larger. This cap is cumulative, per issuer, across every sale of that company's stock you ever claim the exclusion against, not a fresh allowance for each sale.

Which rule applies to my stock?

The rule depends on when you ACQUIRED the stock, not the tax year you sell it in. Stock acquired on or before July 4, 2025 follows the old all-or-nothing rule for its entire life, even if you sell it in 2027 or later. Stock acquired after that date follows the new tiered rule.

Does this verify that my stock actually qualifies as QSBS?

No. Qualifying as QSBS in the first place depends on company-level facts this calculator does not check — original issuance, C-corp status, active-business requirements, and the gross-assets threshold at issuance. This tool only computes the shareholder-level exclusion math once you already know the stock qualifies.

Is this tax advice?

No. This calculator applies the published federal Section 1202 exclusion rules to the numbers you enter. It does not verify QSBS eligibility, track your cumulative prior exclusions against this issuer, or account for day-precision holding-period timing, and it is not a substitute for reviewing IRS guidance or consulting a qualified tax professional before you file.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified tax professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for confirming your own numbers before filing a return. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record — nothing you enter is saved anywhere by this tool.

Everything runs in your browser. Your numbers are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (estimate_calculated, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage on your device. The counts can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

This calculator vs. working out the QSBS exclusion by hand

The arithmetic looks simple — a percentage of a gain. The part that goes wrong by hand is which rule applies to which stock, and what the cap is actually a percentage of.

Where a hand estimate usually goes wrong

StepCommon mistake by handWhat this calculator does
Which rule appliesApplies the new tiered schedule to stock acquired before July 4, 2025.Uses the acquisition date to select the correct rule — old stock keeps the all-or-nothing cliff for its entire life.
The exclusion capUses only the fixed dollar figure, ignoring the 10x-basis alternative.Computes both and uses whichever is greater, as the statute requires.
Order of operationsApplies the holding-period percentage to the full, uncapped gain.Caps eligible gain first, then applies the percentage to that capped figure.
The cap's scopeTreats the cap as a fresh allowance per sale.Flags that the cap is cumulative, per issuer, across every sale — this tool assumes a single, first-ever sale against it.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?N/ANo. The calculator runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent to a server.

Common questions

What's the single most common mistake working this out by hand?

Applying the new tiered 50/75/100% schedule to stock acquired before July 4, 2025. The tiered schedule only applies to stock acquired AFTER that date — earlier stock keeps the old all-or-nothing 5-year cliff for its entire life, no matter when it is eventually sold.

What's the second most common mistake?

Using only the fixed dollar cap ($10 million or $15 million) and forgetting the 10-times-basis alternative. The cap is the GREATER of the two — for a large gain on a small basis (common when basis is low, like an early employee's exercised options), the fixed dollar figure usually governs, but for a large basis it can be the 10x-basis figure that is actually higher.

What arithmetic mistake gets made most often?

Applying the holding-period percentage to the total gain instead of to the CAPPED eligible gain. The cap is applied first to determine eligible gain; the percentage is then applied to that capped figure, not to the full, uncapped sale gain.

What planning mistake gets made most often?

Treating the per-issuer cap as a fresh allowance for every sale. It is cumulative, per issuer, across every sale of that company's stock a taxpayer ever claims the exclusion against — a second sale from the same issuer does not get a second full cap.

Does this calculator know my complete tax situation?

No. Neither this calculator nor a by-hand worksheet built from this page verifies whether the stock actually qualifies as QSBS, tracks your cumulative prior exclusions against this issuer, or accounts for day-precision holding-period timing. Both apply the same published federal rules to the numbers you enter; verify against IRS guidance or a qualified tax professional before relying on either.

No warranty. This page and the linked calculator apply published federal Section 1202 rules to numbers you supply. It is not legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified tax professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for confirming your own numbers before filing a return. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. The calculator this page links to runs entirely client-side; nothing you enter is uploaded anywhere.
